I p3a.text: The first point to which attention should be called is that the comic does not exist outside the pale of what is strictly human.
I p3a.alignment: French claim that comedy lies within the strictly human, with an added opening frame; human is italic in print.

I p4a.text: Here I would point out, as a symptom equally worthy of notice, the absence of feeling which usually accompanies laughter. It seems as though the comic could not produce its disturbing effect unless it fell, so to say, on the surface of a soul that is thoroughly calm and unruffled. Indifference is its natural environment, for laughter has no greater foe than emotion.
I p4a.alignment: Corresponds to the three French propositions; the English sentence includes its additional clause on emotion, required for a whole sentence.

II p95a.text: Picture to yourself certain characters in a certain situation: if you reverse the situation and invert the rôles, you obtain a comic scene.
II p95a.alignment: Reversal of situation and roles corresponds; print has rôles with circumflex and italic emphasis.

II p98a.text: A situation is invariably comic when it belongs simultaneously to two altogether independent series of events and is capable of being interpreted in two entirely different meanings at the same time.
II p98a.alignment: The same two independent series and two interpretations; the English sentence is italic in the printed page.

II p124a.text: And so the play upon words always betrays a momentary lapse of attention in language, and it is precisely on that account that it is amusing.
II p124a.alignment: The French momentary distraction of language becomes a momentary lapse of attention in language.

III p181a.text: Now, it is the business of laughter to repress any separatist tendency. Its function is to convert rigidity into plasticity, to readapt the individual to the whole, in short, to round off the corners wherever they are met with.
III p181a.alignment: Two corresponding sentences; French readapting each to all becomes the individual to the whole.

I p50a.text: Our starting-point is again "something mechanical encrusted upon the living." Where did the comic come from in this case? It came from the fact that the living body became rigid, like a machine.
I p50a.alignment: The three sentences follow the French section marker; the English quotation has upon, as printed.

II p126a.text: Transpose the solemn into the familiar and the result is parody.
II p126a.alignment: The French question and answer are rendered as one complete English sentence about parody.

II p89b.text: The comic is that side of a person which reveals his likeness to a thing, that aspect of human events which, through its peculiar inelasticity, conveys the impression of pure mechanism, of automatism, of movement without life.
II p89b.alignment: First sentence corresponds to the French definition; imitates is rendered conveys the impression.

II p124b.text: Inversion and reciprocal interference, after all, are only a certain playfulness of the mind which ends at playing upon words.
II p124b.alignment: The French inversion and interference leading to wordplay correspond to English reciprocal interference.

I p50b.text: To sum up, then, we have one and the same effect, which assumes ever subtler forms as it passes from the idea of an artificial mechanisation of the human body, if such an expression is permissible, to that of any substitution whatsoever of the artificial for the natural.
I p50b.alignment: The same progressive refinement from artificial mechanisation of the body to artificial replacing natural.

I p3a.alignment: The English combines the preceding introductory sentence with the French proposition; both scans show the proposition and matching human emphasis.

I p4a.alignment: Three English sentences correspond; its final sentence incorporates the next French sentence on emotion, preserving complete English boundaries.

II p95a.alignment: The French sentence runs across pages 95 and 96; the English page 94 renders the same reversal of situation and roles.

II p98a.alignment: Both books introduce this complete definitional formula after a colon; two independent series and two meanings align.

II p124a.alignment: Wordplay betrays a momentary distraction of language, rendered lapse of attention in language; both sentences read as printed.

III p181a.alignment: Two sentences retain the corrective function; each to all is rendered individual to the whole, a shift of phrasing.

I p50a.alignment: The section marker is omitted from English; three complete sentences retain the mechanical on the living and machine comparison.

II p126a.alignment: The French question and answer become one English sentence; the solemn-to-familiar direction and parody remain.

II p89b.alignment: The complete first sentence aligns; French imitates is rendered conveys the impression, a nuance in translation.

II p124b.alignment: Inversion and interference as mental games leading to wordplay align; English calls the interference reciprocal.

I p50b.alignment: The full sentence retains the increasingly subtle effect and substitution of artificial for natural.
